questions.stem: In the first years of life, the brain forms far more synapses than it will keep. What happens to the connections that are rarely used?
options: They are moved to the forebrain for long-term storage
They are eliminated through synaptic pruning
They are covered with a myelin sheath
They are strengthened until they are used
questions.explanation: Synaptic pruning removes weak, rarely used connections, while frequently used ones are kept and strengthened. This 'use it or lose it' process makes the remaining networks more efficient. Myelination insulates axons; it does not remove connections.

questions.stem: Myelination during infancy and adolescence mainly results in:
options: faster transmission of messages along axons
the growth of brand new neurons in the cortex
the removal of unused synapses between neurons
a larger number of dendrites on each neuron
questions.explanation: Myelination wraps axons in a fatty insulating sheath, which speeds up neural transmission and improves coordination and processing. Removing unused synapses is synaptic pruning, a separate process.

questions.stem: Which part of the forebrain is the last to mature, continuing to develop into a person's twenties?
options: the medulla oblongata
the prefrontal cortex
the amygdala
the cerebellum
questions.explanation: The prefrontal cortex, which supports planning, judgement and impulse control, is among the last areas to finish myelination and pruning. The amygdala, involved in emotional responses, matures earlier, and the cerebellum and medulla are not part of the forebrain.

questions.stem: Adolescents often take more risks and react more emotionally than adults. Which explanation is consistent with brain development?
options: Synaptic pruning in adolescence removes the connections used for emotion
Myelination in adolescence slows the transmission of messages in the forebrain
The amygdala matures before the prefrontal cortex that helps regulate it
The prefrontal cortex matures before the amygdala that helps regulate it
questions.explanation: The amygdala, involved in emotional reactions, develops earlier than the prefrontal cortex, which supports judgement and impulse control. Until the prefrontal cortex matures, emotional responses are less well regulated. Myelination speeds transmission rather than slowing it.

questions.stem: Why are infancy and adolescence both described as periods of rapid brain development?
options: Both are the only times in life when new learning changes the brain
Both involve the brain growing new neurons in every region
Both end with the brain no longer able to form synapses
Both involve large changes in synapses, myelination and brain function
questions.explanation: In infancy the brain forms synapses rapidly and myelinates quickly; in adolescence pruning and myelination reorganise it, especially in the forebrain. Plasticity continues throughout life, so these are not the only periods when learning changes the brain.

questions.stem: Neural plasticity is best defined as the brain's ability to:
options: keep a fixed set of neural connections throughout the life span
send messages faster as axons become myelinated
grow back exactly the same neurons after an injury
change its structure and function in response to experience
questions.explanation: Plasticity means the brain physically changes, forming, strengthening and losing connections, as a result of experience, learning and injury. It is greatest in early life but continues throughout the life span.

questions.stem: Young rats raised in large cages with toys, tunnels and other rats are compared with rats raised alone in bare cages. What would brain development research predict?
options: The rats in the enriched cages develop more synaptic connections
The rats in the bare cages develop more synaptic connections
Both groups develop the same connections because genes fix brain growth
The rats in the enriched cages develop fewer, but larger, neurons
questions.explanation: An enriched environment provides stimulation that encourages synapses to form and strengthen, giving a thicker, more connected cortex. A deprived environment gives fewer opportunities to use connections, so more are pruned. Experience, not genes alone, shapes brain development.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a sensitive period and a critical period in development?
options: A sensitive period is for physical skills; a critical period is for social skills
A sensitive period is optimal for learning; a critical period is the only window
A critical period is optimal for learning; a sensitive period is the only window
A sensitive period happens in adolescence; a critical period happens in old age
questions.explanation: During a sensitive period the brain is especially responsive to certain experiences, but the skill can still be learnt later, less easily. In a critical period, if the experience does not occur, the ability may never develop normally.

questions.stem: A child born with cataracts in both eyes has them removed at age eight. Even with clear lenses, the child's vision remains impaired. Which concept best explains this?
options: A sensitive period for language development was missed
Synaptic pruning had not yet started in the visual cortex
Myelination of the visual system was too rapid in infancy
A critical period for the visual system was missed
questions.explanation: The visual system needs input during a critical period early in life to wire up normally; without it, later correction cannot fully restore vision. Language is not involved here, and pruning would already have occurred.

questions.stem: After a stroke damages an area that controls her right hand, Lena slowly regains use of the hand with therapy. How does plasticity explain her recovery?
options: Myelin grows over the damaged area and replaces the lost neurons
Undamaged neurons form new connections and take over some lost functions
The damaged neurons regrow quickly and restore their original connections
The brain prunes the damaged neurons so the hand no longer needs them
questions.explanation: After brain damage, undamaged neurons can sprout new branches and form new connections, so nearby areas take over some functions. Damaged neurons in the brain generally do not regrow their original connections, and myelin cannot replace neurons.

questions.stem: A five-year-old and a fifty-year-old suffer similar damage to the same brain area. Which outcome is most likely, and why?
options: The adult recovers more function, because adult neurons are fully myelinated
Both recover equally, because plasticity is constant across the life span
Neither recovers any function, because the brain cannot change after damage
The child recovers more function, because the young brain is more plastic
questions.explanation: Plasticity is greatest early in life, when synapses are abundant and pruning is still under way, so a child's brain can more readily reorganise to take over lost functions. Adults also show plasticity, but usually less, so recovery is typically more limited.

questions.stem: In developmental psychology, attachment is:
options: a close emotional bond between an infant and a caregiver
an infant's ability to recognise faces from a few days old
the stage when a child first begins to use words to name objects
the process by which a child learns to share with others
questions.explanation: Attachment is the strong emotional bond that forms between an infant and their main caregivers, giving the child a secure base from which to explore. Face recognition and language are separate aspects of development.

questions.stem: Konrad Lorenz (1937) observed that newly hatched goslings would follow the first moving object they saw, including Lorenz himself. This process is called:
options: contact comfort
scaffolding
assimilation
imprinting
questions.explanation: Imprinting is a rapid form of attachment that occurs during a brief critical period soon after hatching. Contact comfort comes from Harlow's research on monkeys, and scaffolding and assimilation belong to theories of cognitive development.

questions.stem: In the research of Harlow and Zimmermann (1958), infant rhesus monkeys could choose between a wire surrogate mother with a feeding bottle and a soft cloth surrogate with no food. What did the monkeys' behaviour show?
options: The monkeys attached to whichever surrogate they saw first
Contact comfort mattered more to attachment than being fed
Being fed mattered more to attachment than contact comfort
The monkeys formed no attachment to either surrogate mother
questions.explanation: The monkeys spent most of their time clinging to the cloth surrogate and ran to it when frightened, visiting the wire one only to feed. This contradicted the idea that attachment forms simply because the mother provides food.

questions.stem: John Bowlby's attachment theory (1969) proposed that infants are born with a need to form an attachment because:
options: children learn to love whichever adult rewards them most often with food
infants attach only to adults who speak to them in their own first language
babies copy the attachment behaviour they see in older brothers and sisters
staying close to a caregiver helped infants survive and so was favoured by evolution
questions.explanation: Bowlby argued attachment is an evolved, innate system: infants who kept caregivers close were protected and more likely to survive. He rejected the view that attachment is simply learnt through being fed.

questions.stem: According to Bowlby, a child's early attachment relationship forms an internal working model. This is:
options: a list of rules the child learns about acceptable behaviour
a stage of thinking in which the child can reverse operations
a method a caregiver uses to support the child's learning
a mental template of relationships that guides later ones
questions.explanation: The internal working model is a set of expectations about oneself, others and relationships that grows from early attachment and shapes later relationships. Reversing operations is a feature of Piaget's concrete operational stage.

questions.stem: In the Strange Situation procedure of Ainsworth and colleagues (1978), what is the main behaviour observed to classify an infant's attachment?
options: Whether the infant can find a toy hidden under a blanket
How many words the infant uses with a stranger present
How the infant responds when the caregiver leaves and returns
How quickly the infant learns to solve a simple puzzle
questions.explanation: The procedure uses short separations and reunions with the caregiver and a stranger, focusing especially on how the infant behaves at reunion. Finding a hidden toy tests object permanence, which is a Piagetian concept.

questions.stem: Over several decades, ideas about attachment changed: Lorenz showed rapid imprinting in birds, Harlow showed the role of contact comfort, Bowlby built an evolutionary theory, and Ainsworth devised a way to measure attachment types. What does this sequence best illustrate?
options: Each researcher disproved all of the findings of those before them
Animal studies alone are enough to establish theories about humans
Theories in psychology are fixed once the first study is published
Researchers build on and challenge the work of earlier researchers
questions.explanation: Each contribution extended or challenged earlier ideas: Bowlby drew on animal research such as Lorenz's and Harlow's, and Ainsworth tested his theory in humans. Later work refined rather than wholly disproved what came before.

questions.stem: Which outcome is most consistent with research on children raised from infancy in severely depriving institutions with little individual care?
options: Delays in language and thinking, and difficulties forming attachments
Faster language development, because the children learn to be independent
No lasting effects, provided the children's physical needs were met
Improved memory, because the children have fewer distractions
questions.explanation: Severe early deprivation is linked to delays in cognitive and language development, and to difficulties forming close relationships. Meeting physical needs such as food is not enough; children also need responsive care and stimulation for normal development.

questions.stem: Children who are removed from a severely deprived environment and placed in a caring family early tend to recover better than those placed later. Which concept best explains this?
options: Synaptic pruning, which adds many new connections once deprivation ends
The internal working model, which forms only after the age of ten
Metacognition, which allows the child to plan a recovery strategy
Sensitive periods, when the brain is especially responsive to experience
questions.explanation: Early childhood includes sensitive periods when the brain is especially plastic, so enriched care at that time has the greatest effect. Pruning removes connections rather than adding them, and the internal working model forms early, not after ten.

questions.stem: Research with children who have suffered abuse must follow strict ethical principles. Which practice is most important for protecting these participants?
options: Recording identifying details so other researchers can follow up later
Exposing the children to stressful tasks to measure the effects of abuse
Ensuring informed consent from guardians, confidentiality and freedom to withdraw
Using deception so the children do not know the true purpose of the study
questions.explanation: Vulnerable participants need consent from a parent or guardian, protection of their identity, and the right to stop at any time without penalty. Deception, sharing identifying details or causing further distress would breach ethical principles.

questions.stem: Which theorist is most closely associated with the idea that children develop through social interaction within a zone of proximal development?
options: Harry Harlow
Lev Vygotsky
Jean Piaget
Konrad Lorenz
questions.explanation: Vygotsky's sociocultural theory centres on learning with the guidance of more knowledgeable others within the zone of proximal development. Piaget focused on stages of individual discovery, and Lorenz and Harlow studied attachment in animals.

questions.stem: Which statement about neural plasticity across the life span is correct?
options: It occurs only after the brain has been damaged by injury
It is greatest in early childhood but continues into old age
It occurs only in infancy and stops completely by adolescence
It is weakest in early childhood and greatest in old age
questions.explanation: The brain is most plastic early in life, when synapses are forming and being pruned rapidly, but it keeps changing with learning and experience throughout life. Plasticity is not limited to recovery from damage.

questions.stem: Which psychologist proposed that children's thinking develops through four stages, from sensorimotor to formal operational?
options: Mary Ainsworth
Jean Piaget
Lev Vygotsky
John Bowlby
questions.explanation: Jean Piaget's cognitive theory describes the sensorimotor, preoperational, concrete operational and formal operational stages. Vygotsky emphasised social and cultural influences, and Bowlby and Ainsworth studied attachment.

questions.stem: Four-year-old Sam pretends a banana is a telephone and chats into it, but he assumes his friend can see the same view of a picture that he can. Which of Piaget's stages is Sam most likely in?
options: sensorimotor
concrete operational
formal operational
preoperational
questions.explanation: Using one object to stand for another shows symbolic thinking, and assuming others see what he sees shows egocentrism; both are typical of the preoperational stage, about two to seven years. Children in the sensorimotor stage do not yet use symbols in pretend play like this.

questions.stem: A toddler sees a horse for the first time and calls it 'doggy' because it has four legs and fur. In Piaget's terms, the child has:
options: accommodated the horse by creating a new schema
conserved the horse's features despite its size
internalised the horse through private speech
assimilated the horse into an existing schema
questions.explanation: Assimilation is fitting a new experience into an existing schema, here the schema for 'dog'. Accommodation would happen when the child changes the schema and recognises the horse as a different kind of animal.

questions.stem: A child understands that a toy still exists when it is hidden under a cloth. In which of Piaget's stages does this ability, object permanence, develop?
options: sensorimotor
preoperational
concrete operational
formal operational
questions.explanation: Object permanence develops during the sensorimotor stage, roughly birth to two years, as infants learn through their senses and actions. By the preoperational stage children already have it.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes Piaget's concrete operational stage from his formal operational stage?
options: Concrete thinkers cannot yet conserve; formal thinkers can conserve number and volume
Concrete thinkers are egocentric; formal thinkers can take another person's view
Concrete thinkers reason logically about real objects; formal thinkers also reason abstractly
Concrete thinkers reason abstractly; formal thinkers reason only about real objects
questions.explanation: In the concrete operational stage children can conserve and reason logically, but mainly about concrete situations. In the formal operational stage they can also reason about abstract and hypothetical ideas. Conservation and overcoming egocentrism are already achieved in the concrete stage.

questions.stem: Vygotsky's sociocultural theory emphasises that cognitive development is driven mainly by:
options: biological maturation through a fixed series of universal stages
the number of synapses a child forms in infancy
rewards and punishments given for correct answers
social interaction and the tools and language of a culture
questions.explanation: Vygotsky argued that children develop through interaction with more knowledgeable people and by taking on the language and tools of their culture. A fixed series of stages driven by maturation is closer to Piaget's view.

questions.stem: In Vygotsky's theory, the zone of proximal development is:
options: the age range during which a child develops object permanence
the part of the brain that matures during adolescence
the set of skills a child has already fully mastered on their own
the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with help
questions.explanation: The zone of proximal development covers tasks a child cannot yet do independently but can achieve with guidance. Skills already mastered alone lie below the zone, so teaching within the zone is what drives development.

questions.stem: Ella, aged six, cannot tie her shoelaces alone. Her older brother shows her each step, then gradually gives less help until she can do it herself. In Vygotsky's terms, the brother is acting as:
options: an attachment figure who gives her a secure base from which to explore
a model whose behaviour she learns only through rewards and punishments
a more knowledgeable other providing support in her zone of proximal development
a peer who prevents her from developing her own schemas through discovery
questions.explanation: The brother has more skill than Ella and adjusts his help to what she can manage, withdrawing it as she becomes competent. This is guided support within her zone of proximal development, which Vygotsky saw as the engine of cognitive growth.

questions.stem: Which statement best contrasts Piaget's and Vygotsky's views of how children learn?
options: Piaget saw children as discovering alone; Vygotsky stressed learning with others
Piaget stressed learning with others; Vygotsky saw children as discovering alone
Piaget said culture shapes thinking; Vygotsky said development is the same in all cultures
Piaget denied that stages exist; Vygotsky proposed four universal stages
questions.explanation: Piaget described the child as a 'little scientist' constructing knowledge through their own exploration, in universal stages. Vygotsky emphasised social interaction, language and culture, so development could differ between cultures. Vygotsky did not propose four universal stages.

questions.stem: Information processing theories compare cognitive development to:
options: a plant that grows only when it receives social support
a set of habits learned through rewards and punishments
a computer that improves in speed, capacity and strategies
a series of separate stages that every child passes through
questions.explanation: Information processing theories treat the mind like a computer that takes in, stores and retrieves information, and see development as gradual improvement in processing speed, strategies and metacognition. Fixed stages belong to Piaget's theory.

questions.stem: As children get older, they can respond to questions and solve simple problems more quickly. Which biological change best explains this increase in processing speed?
options: Increasing numbers of unused synapses
Decreasing size of the prefrontal cortex
Decreasing activity in the hindbrain
Increasing myelination of axons
questions.explanation: Myelination speeds the transmission of impulses, so information moves through the brain faster with age. A larger number of unused synapses would make networks less efficient, which is why pruning removes them.

questions.stem: To learn a list of words for a test, Noah groups them into categories such as fruit, tools and animals. In information processing theory, this is an example of:
options: metacognition
faster processing speed
object permanence
a cognitive strategy
questions.explanation: Cognitive strategies are deliberate methods to improve thinking and memory, such as rehearsal or organising information into categories. Metacognition would be Noah thinking about whether his method is working.

questions.stem: After a practice test, Zoe realises she understands photosynthesis well but not respiration, so she spends more time studying respiration. This shows:
options: assimilation
imprinting
metacognition
processing speed
questions.explanation: Metacognition is thinking about one's own thinking: knowing what you know and don't know, and adjusting your approach. It improves through childhood and adolescence and is a key part of information processing theories.

questions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes information processing theories from Piaget's theory?
options: They see development as driven mainly by social interaction and culture
They see development as ending once a child reaches adolescence
They see development as gradual and continuous rather than in distinct stages
They see development as occurring in four distinct, universal stages
questions.explanation: Information processing theories describe steady, continuous improvements in speed, strategies and metacognition, rather than qualitative leaps between stages as in Piaget's theory. An emphasis on social interaction and culture is Vygotsky's view.
